'''Kasso Akochayé Okoudjou''' is a [[Benin]]ese-American mathematician and Professor of Mathematics at [[Tufts University]]. His research spans [[harmonic analysis]], [[time–frequency analysis]], and [[fractal]]s, with particular focus on [[Frame (linear algebra)|frame theory]] and its applications to [[signal processing]] and [[quantum information]]. He is a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/fellows_by_year.cgi?year=2024|title=2024 Class of Fellows of the AMS|publisher=American Mathematical Society|access-date=2023-11-09}}</ref> and served as the 2018 [[Martin Luther King Jr.|Martin Luther King]] Visiting professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="Kasso Akochayé Okoudjou">{{Cite web|title=Kasso Akochayé Okoudjou|url=https://mlkscholars.mit.edu/scholars/kasso-akochay-okoudjou|access-date=2021-04-21|website=MIT MLK Visiting Scholars & Professors Program}}</ref>

== Education ==

Okoudjou studied mathematics at the [[University of Abomey-Calavi]] in [[Benin]], earning a [[maîtrise]] in 1996.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://okoudjou.com/files/2020/11/Okoudjou_PubCV.pdf|title=Curriculum vitae|access-date=2025-08-28}}</ref> After graduating, he worked as an instructor at the Complexe Scolaire William Ponty de Porto-Novo.<ref name=":0" /> In 1998 he began graduate studies at the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]], where he earned his PhD in 2003 with a dissertation on the characterization of function spaces and bilinear [[pseudodifferential operator]]s through [[Gabor frame]]s, supervised by Christopher Edward Heil.<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref> His thesis received the [[Sigma Xi]] Best PhD Thesis Award.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==

After completing his doctorate, Okoudjou was appointed H. C. Wang Assistant Professor at [[Cornell University]] in 2003. He spent 2005 at the [[Erwin Schrödinger International Institute for Mathematical Physics]] in Vienna, then joined the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] in 2006.<ref name=":0" /> He served as the Martin Luther King Visiting professor at MIT from 2017 to 2019, and moved to [[Tufts University]] in 2020, where he is Professor of Mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kasso A. Okoudjou's webpage|url=https://sites.tufts.edu/kasso/|access-date=2021-04-21|website=sites.tufts.edu|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research ==

Okoudjou's research centers on harmonic analysis, time–frequency analysis, and fractal geometry. A major strand of his work involves [[Frame (linear algebra)|frame theory]], which concerns redundant representations of data. He has applied frame-theoretic methods to problems in digital signal processing and [[quantum information]], with conditional results drawing on the [[SIC-POVM#Zauner's conjecture|Zauner conjecture]] and the [[Heil–Ramanathan–Topiwala conjecture]]. In 2018, he received a [[National Science Foundation]] grant to study finite [[Gabor system]]s and related conjectures.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1814253&HistoricalAwards=false|title=NSF Award Search: Award#1814253 - Two Conjectures on Finite Gabor Systems|website=nsf.gov|access-date=2018-12-06}}</ref>

=== Books ===

* {{Cite book|last=Okoudjou|first=Kasso A.|title=Finite Frame Theory: A Complete Introduction to Overcompleteness|year=2016|series=Proceedings of Symposia in Applied Mathematics|isbn=9781470420192}}

== Service and advocacy ==

In June 2020, Okoudjou was appointed co-chair of the [[American Mathematical Society]] task force on racial discrimination, established in the wake of [[2020–2021 United States racial unrest|a nationwide reckoning on racial justice in the United States]]. The task force published its report, "Towards a Fully Inclusive Mathematics Profession," in March 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Towards a fully inclusive mathematics profession|url=https://www.ams.org/about-us/understanding-ams-history|access-date=2021-04-21|website=American Mathematical Society|language=en}}</ref>
